lafferHistory.finding: The curve even has a napkin: on 13 September 1974, in a Washington restaurant, the economist Arthur Laffer drew the hill on a napkin to convince Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney that the Ford administration's tax rise would backfire. The journalist Jude Wanniski kept the napkin — it is now in the Smithsonian — and christened the idea the 'Laffer Curve' in a 1978 article.
lafferDebate[0].finding: Where is the top? The most cited academic estimate (Trabandt & Uhlig, 2011) puts the peak for labour taxation at effective rates of ~50% to 70% — most rich countries sit on the left side of the hill. The curve is real; the top is high and varies by tax.
lafferDebate[1].finding: And the other side: tax cuts rarely 'pay for themselves'. Reagan's 1981 cut cost ~US$ 750 billion in revenue between 1981 and 1986, according to the US government itself. Using the hill to justify any cut is as dishonest as ignoring it to justify any rise.
lafferDebate[2].finding: And Brazil? An academic study (UEL, 2017) estimated, for 1996-2014, the point at which Brazilian revenue would be at its maximum: a burden of ~40.7% of GDP — above today's 32.4%, but with less headroom than it looks, because the calculation ignores what comes back in services. Another study, by the Treasury, found evidence of the curve in Rio Grande do Sul's state VAT: rate rises with ever smaller returns. It is a field with few studies and many caveats — which is why the hill in the drawing is a concept, not a map.
brazilCases[0].finding: The tax on cigarettes in Brazil is 71% of the price; in Paraguay, 13%. The result: consumers moved to smuggling and the government loses billions — the wrong side of the hill, via evasion.
